gen-eater-gf-courier-prime: Courier Prime reads like a drafting pen at work, a monospace with generous round letters and lowercase that fills the line. And Eater sets it off with moody, uneven strokes, thin parts and stems clearly different, against that single-thickness line.
gen-eater-gf-days-one: Days One sets its letters out like rungs on a rope ladder, with a tall x-height that fills each line to the edges. Eater brings the gloom up top, and the sturdy sans below steadies it.
gen-eater-gf-epunda-sans: Eater arrives dark and aggressive, with a moderate stroke contrast that still reads easily. But Epunda Sans, a plain sans with oversized, daylight-filled curves, is what gives the pair its pull.
gen-eater-gf-farro: Approachable first, Farro draws every line like bent tubing with no stroke contrast at all. Under Eater's dark, gap-toothed headings, a longer passage would move along smoothly, with short ascenders keeping the lines compact and tidy.
gen-eater-gf-fragment-mono: Fragment Mono lays its letters out like nails on a ruler, a monospace with a tall waist line. Fragment Mono's smooth, wire-like line would carry a long passage without a snag, while Eater's sturdy thin parts supply the menace above.
gen-eater-gf-geist-mono: Eater's strokes sit between monoline and sharp contrast, with wide gaps between letters. Geist Mono, a monospace with high-rising lowercase and generous side gaps, gives the pair its strongest quality: dark swagger set over structured, technical order.
gen-eater-gf-genos: Eater opens dark and aggressive, with wide gaps between its letters. Genos, a sans-serif with a high-set midline, packs its glyphs tightly and reads smoothly, which is the pair's sharpest difference.
gen-eater-gf-geom: Hairline-free thin strokes, set against moderately weighty stems, give Eater its menace. Geom, a plain sans with a lofty lowercase band, stays approachable beneath it, and that mix of gloom and friendliness is the pair's strongest quality.
gen-eater-gf-hammersmith-one: Wide letter-to-letter gaps give Eater its dark, aggressive drawl. Hammersmith One, a sans-serif with rounded strokes like cut lengths of cord and capitals barely taller than lowercase, softens the page below it.
gen-eater-gf-inder: Inder barely separates its capitals from its lowercase, a plain sans that reads clean and level. Inder gives Eater's shimmering, weight-shifting headings somewhere quiet to land, so the dark display type never has to compete.
